stories.headline: California Governor Newsom Commutes Death Sentences of All 548 Death Row Inmates
stories.summary:
California Governor Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 people on the state's death row, converting them to life in prison without the possibility of parole. He announced the move in a letter, saying: "We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honour the victims." California has the largest death row population in the country.

Newsom said he was using his constitutional clemency authority. He called the state's system of capital punishment "a failure" that has not and cannot be fairly applied, and said it has resulted in the conviction of innocent people. "The state cannot morally kill them," he wrote, describing the decision as difficult but a "righteous action" that he alone bears responsibility for. He acknowledged it would anger and hurt some Californians.

The practical effect is largely symbolic: California has not executed a prisoner since 2006, and only 13 inmates have been put to death since voters reinstated the death penalty in 1978. Newsom had already ordered a moratorium on executions in 2019. Experts say the change could save the state millions of dollars a year in court costs.

The decision comes as Newsom, who is term limited and in his final months in office, is discussed as a possible 2028 presidential contender. Democrat Xavier Becerra is projected to succeed him. Supporters of capital punishment, including President Donald Trump, who has called it an essential tool for deterring and punishing heinous crimes, are likely to criticize the move, while opponents of the death penalty are expected to praise it.

stories.headline: Eight Killed in Series of Shootings in Western Turkey; Suspect Arrested
stories.summary:
Eight people were killed and one seriously injured in a series of shootings in Turkey's Afyonkarahisar province on Thursday. Victims were found in several locations in three separate vehicles, according to local reports. Two teachers were reportedly among the dead.

State-run Anadolu Agency reported that three people were killed near Ayazini village and three others near Kiyir village. In Yukaritandir, two women were found injured and later died in hospital. CCTV footage published in Turkish media showed a man in a black jacket and white trousers holding a long weapon beside a red minivan.

The suspect fled, prompting a large manhunt with roads to the affected villages closed. Milliyet reported that a vehicle allegedly taken by the attacker was later found stuck in mud, and that he abandoned it and fled on foot. Authorities later said he was arrested in neighbouring Eskisehir province.

The Afyonkarahisar Governorate said all relevant state institutions had been coordinating since the first moment. No motive has been given.

stories.headline: Shooting at Des Moines Post Office Leaves Three Injured; Suspect in Custody
stories.summary:
Three people were injured in a shooting at the main U.S. Postal Service facility in Des Moines, Iowa, on Thursday, and a suspect is in custody. Police said they began receiving multiple calls around 9:10 a.m. reporting an active killer on the second floor of the building on Second Avenue. Officers arrived within three minutes.

Des Moines Police Sgt. Paul Parizek said three victims were known and had been taken to hospitals. Their injuries were initially believed to be non-life-threatening, though their condition had not been confirmed. "We were able to get here quickly and make sure that we stopped the killing before it got any worse," he said.

The ATF and FBI joined local police at the scene, and the public was asked to avoid the area. The motive was not immediately clear. Gov. Kim Reynolds said she was monitoring the situation and thanked law enforcement for their immediate response, and Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa, offered prayers for the victims.

stories.headline: Update: Hoax Bomb Threats Target European Flights and Airports for Second Time This Week
stories.summary:
At least 21 aircraft and several airports across Europe were targeted by bomb threats on Thursday, the second such wave this week. Flights to Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, France, Italy, Poland and Romania were affected. The UK government called the threats a "malicious hoax," and no explosives were found in any searches.

An Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to an air base in France, landing safely in Normandy, and Italian fighter jets escorted a Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome. EasyJet flights from Newcastle and Glasgow were met by police in Prague as a precaution. Heathrow and Birmingham airports received threats that were assessed as not credible.

Aeroporti di Roma said emails warning of the threats to two inbound flights were signed by "Fighters of the Male State," which claimed to target a "feminist regime" and threatened to "turn the skies red." The name likely refers to the Russian ultra-right group "Muzhskoi Legion," banned by a Moscow court in 2021, though investigators may not be able to trace the source. UK Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said the government takes such threats seriously and has established processes for handling them.

stories.headline: Paraguay President Santiago Peña Resigns After Collapse of Bank Linked to Him
stories.summary:
Paraguay's President Santiago Peña announced his resignation following a political crisis sparked by the collapse of Ueno Bank, a digital lender tied to him. In a video message posted on X, he apologized to the public, saying, "It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me." He said stepping down was meant to protect stability, social peace and democratic institutions.

The crisis began when Ueno Bank entered an insolvency process that froze all operations. The bank says it has about three million customers, roughly 60 percent of Paraguay's adult population, and it held pensions and some other public funds. Millions of people were unable to access their accounts after the central bank seized the lender earlier this week, and protesters took to the streets demanding Peña's resignation.

Lawmakers accused Peña, who was a shareholder until last year in the company that owned the bank, of conflicts of interest and misconduct. Peña has rejected suggestions of impropriety. His resignation came after the lower house of Congress voted to pursue an impeachment trial.

A new president of the Central Bank of Paraguay has been appointed, and Congress has approved a process to pay depositors. Peña, of the ruling conservative Colorado Party, won election in 2023 over a centre-left challenger. Attention now turns to the succession and to whether depositors are repaid.

stories.headline: Harmeet Dhillon Resigns as Head of Justice Department Civil Rights Division
stories.summary:
Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general for civil rights, has resigned, Attorney General Todd Blanche announced Thursday. Blanche said he accepted the resignation of Dhillon, who led the division "with conviction the past 18 months" and "defended the civil liberties of every American." She is the first senior Justice Department official to depart since Democrats won control of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections.

Axios reported that Dhillon spent her tenure replacing attorneys with others more closely aligned with the Trump administration's ideology. Supporters credit her with pursuing the administration's civil rights priorities, while critics say she reshaped the division along political lines. The Washington Examiner, citing two people familiar with the matter, reported that Dhillon had told allies she planned to leave after the midterms.

The departure comes as the administration faces a changed political landscape, with Democrats set to take over House committees in January and promising oversight of the executive branch. It also arrives as Republicans debate their direction after heavy losses. Who will succeed Dhillon, and whether other senior officials follow her out, has not been announced.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Says He Will Keep Hegseth as Massie Moves to Force Impeachment Vote
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump said Thursday he does not intend to remove Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, even as Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, said he plans to call a House vote to impeach him. Trump acknowledged that the Iran war affected the midterm elections but said he is not considering replacing the Pentagon chief despite voter dissatisfaction. He also conceded it would be easier to confirm a new defense secretary before Democrats take control of Congress next year.

Massie, who has sparred with his own party over the past year, told CNN his impeachment push is "a much gentler version" of what could happen once Democrats hold the majority. The resolution awaits the House when it returns next week. Democrats, who won both chambers on Tuesday, have signaled they intend to use oversight powers aggressively.

The debate follows an extraordinary public break within the Republican Party. Vice President JD Vance wrote on X that "the reason we lost is the war," blaming the administration's Iran campaign for the party's losses, a position that put him at odds with the president. Axios reported that the results also jeopardize Republican plans to use budget reconciliation to fund projects such as Golden Dome.

Trump's defenders argue the administration's military actions were necessary and that Hegseth has carried out the president's policy. Critics in both parties say the war and Pentagon leadership drove voters away from Republicans.

stories.headline: Update: Melania Trump Hosts Russian and Ukrainian Delegations After Brokering Oleshky Evacuation Ceasefire
stories.summary:
First lady Melania Trump hosted representatives from Russia and Ukraine at the White House on Thursday to mark a humanitarian ceasefire around the Ukrainian city of Oleshky. The short-lived local truce allowed civilians to be evacuated and some families to reunite after 1,711 days apart. She praised both sides for choosing "humanity over war" and expressed hope the effort would inspire progress toward a "more enduring" peace.

Both Moscow and Kyiv said Mrs. Trump's team was the driving force behind the evacuation of the besieged city, and analysts noted it was also in both governments' interest to give her a humanitarian win. She urged the delegations to build on the arrangement. No wider ceasefire has been announced.

Fighting elsewhere continued. Russia said Thursday it struck a postal logistics hub, a power substation and a cargo ship, while Ukrainian drones set off fires in an industrial zone in Ryazan, about 200 km southeast of Moscow. Earlier this week Zelensky described Russian strikes on a southeastern Ukrainian village, including a school used as a shelter, as among the deadliest attacks of the war.

stories.headline: Update: Republicans Turn on Trump and Each Other as Democrats Prepare to Take Congress
stories.summary:
Two days after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, Republicans are assigning blame for the losses and Democrats are laying out how they will use their new power. Fox News Digital reported that GOP operatives and donors point first to President Donald Trump. Donor Dan Eberhart called the result "a Trump loss," and one aide cited his "primary revenge tour" against senators, his backing of Ken Paxton and Sen. Darline Graham, and his fight with Sen. Thom Tillis. Democrats flipped seven Senate seats, with Alaska and Mississippi still uncalled, and picked up about 27 House seats.

Vice President JD Vance wrote on X that "the reason we lost is the war," blaming the Iran campaign. Trump has acknowledged the war cost Republicans votes but said he would have done it anyway. Oil prices fell about $8 a barrel after Vance's post on hopes of an offramp. Trump has said he intends to keep Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, though he acknowledged a replacement would be easier to confirm before Democrats take control in January. Other Republicans, including Sen. Ted Cruz and Gov. Ron DeSantis, called the results a rebuke of the president and Congress and urged a focus on affordability.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries launched his bid for speaker, with House Democratic leadership elections set for Nov. 18. Speaker Mike Johnson will not seek the minority leader post, and Majority Leader Steve Scalise has announced his candidacy, with Rep. Jim Jordan floated as a rival. Incoming Oversight Chair Robert Garcia told Trump officials to "lawyer up," and Democrats also say they will target tariffs and restore health subsidies.

Trump has said he will use his veto and also work with Democrats. Democrats lack the two-thirds majority needed to override a veto. Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Republicans will work with Trump against what he called "Democrat extremism." The Mississippi Senate race between Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democrat Scott Colom remains too close to call.

stories.headline: Update: Iran War Becomes Central Issue After Midterms as Trump Weighs Deal or Renewed Strikes
stories.summary:
The midterm results have put new pressure on President Trump over the war with Iran, now in its ninth month. Exit polling by ABC News found 34% of voters called the war crucial to their vote. Vance and Trump have both linked the Republican losses to the conflict, and Axios reported that Trump now must choose between a deal and a return to bombing.

Axios described every option as problematic. Renewed strikes would be unpopular and would likely keep gas prices high, while negotiations could fail if Iranian officials refuse concessions or see weakness. Crude had traded as high as $118 a barrel on Friday before falling sharply on Wednesday. Iranian officials welcomed the Democratic victories as a sign of opposition to the war, and Iran's Revolutionary Guard had urged Americans last month to vote against Trump.

Democrats say they will try to rein in the war through Congress, though they lack veto-proof majorities and fuel prices depend on global oil markets. Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand listed ending the war among Democratic priorities, while Republicans such as Thune have said they will keep working with the president. Rep. Thomas Massie has filed articles of impeachment, which Democrats could adopt in the House but would need Republican support to advance in the Senate.

The U.S. recently carried out strikes on Iranian targets near the Strait of Hormuz, including Qeshm Island. Reports of a series of such attacks before the election have raised questions about transparency. Iran's leadership, including Mojtaba Khamenei's consultations, appears to be moving to a new decision-making system, and the two sides have signaled willingness to keep talking.

stories.headline: Russell Brand Convicted of Rape and Sexual Assault in London
stories.summary:
A jury in London found comedian and actor Russell Brand, 51, guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was cleared of three other charges. He had faced three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault.

The charges dated from 1999 to 2009 and concerned six women, all of whom are entitled to lifelong anonymity. Brand has been remanded in custody. The judge said he would receive significant custodial time.

Sentencing is scheduled for Monday. Brand rose to fame as a comedian and film actor and later became a popular YouTube commentator.

stories.headline: Update: Hong Kong Court Sentences Activist Joshua Wong to 10 More Years Under National Security Law
stories.summary:
A Hong Kong court sentenced pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong, 30, to 10 more years in prison under the Beijing-imposed national security law. It is his second conviction under the law, and the sentence came two months before he was due to be released.

Critics say the case reflects the crackdown on the city's once-thriving pro-democracy movement. Wong is among hundreds of Hongkongers detained under the law, and the sentence underscores authorities' determination to keep the era of mass protests in the past.

Rep. John Moolenaar, a Michigan Republican who chairs the House Select Committee on China, condemned the sentence and called Wong a hero who stood up to an authoritarian superpower.

stories.headline: France Braces for Mass Strikes and Protests as Five Unions Launch National Day of Action
stories.summary:
Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators are expected to march across France on Thursday as five unions from the public and private sectors join a national day of strikes and protests. Authorities expect 500,000 to 700,000 participants nationwide, with tens of thousands in Paris alone. More than 250 separate actions are planned, and some disruption has been reported in schools, hospitals and public transport.

The protests began in September with high school students complaining about poor conditions and resources in education, and have since widened to include a revived yellow-vest movement and workers demanding higher wages to offset the cost of living. The unions are seeking a rise in the minimum wage, currently 12.31 euros an hour, and protection of public services. CFDT head Marylise Leon asked for a net increase of 100 euros a month, while union leader Sophie Binet called it a "great day of convergence" and said "the strike must take over." The education ministry said 81 high schools were shut on Thursday morning and about 17.5 percent of primary schools were affected.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said 70,000 police and gendarmes are being deployed and promised "an extremely firm response" to any violence, following unrest in towns and cities on 17 October. Workers have been asked to halt production at oil refineries, and France is expected to import more electricity than it produces because of disruption at nuclear plants.

The government has tried to ease public anger by releasing 10 million barrels of diesel from strategic reserves to lower fuel costs, and has promised students it will reform the unpopular Parcoursup university admissions platform and replace it by 2028. The yellow-vest movement has called for further blockades on Friday and Saturday, suggesting the pressure on the government will continue beyond Thursday.

stories.headline: Democrat Gina Hinojosa Ousts Texas Gov. Greg Abbott in Upset
stories.summary:
Democrat Gina Hinojosa has defeated incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott in the Texas governor's race, according to the Associated Press. The upset will make her the state's first Latina governor and ends a long run of Republican control of the governor's office.

The result was one of the most striking outcomes of a midterm night in which Democrats took control of both the House and the Senate. BBC reporting noted that some of the biggest swings toward Democrats came in Texas, where the party also won a Senate seat. Democrats additionally flipped Senate seats in South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa, Ohio and Maine.

Exit polling cited by the BBC indicated that the economy was voters' top concern, followed by the state of democracy, and that about two-thirds of voters believed President Donald Trump's policies had worsened economic conditions. Republicans have generally argued that their policies support growth and have pointed to local factors and midterm patterns that historically favor the party out of power. Democrats have framed the results as a rejection of the administration's economic record.

The Texas outcome carries national weight because of the state's size, its electoral votes and its role as a Republican stronghold. Details on the margin and on how the result will affect the state legislature and policy agenda had not yet been reported.

stories.headline: Update: US Conducts Defensive Strikes on Iranian Targets in Strait of Hormuz
stories.summary:
A U.S. official said the United States has conducted defensive strikes on some Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian state television reported that explosions were heard on Qeshm Island, and injuries were reported on both sides.

The strikes follow U.S. attacks on Qeshm Island on the eve of the midterm elections, the first since a two-month pause. They come as the broader U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran continues to grind on, with BBC analysis asking whether either side has an exit strategy and noting that none of Iran's choices offers a clear path to victory.

The conflict has had wide effects, including strikes on commercial vessels and reduced diesel exports from the Middle East. A U.S. aircraft carrier has remained at sea on one of the longest deployments ever. Earlier this week, both Washington and Tehran signaled willingness to keep talking, with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian citing expanded authority.

The U.S. describes its latest actions as defensive, while Iranian media portrayed them as attacks on its territory. The new exchange raises questions about whether diplomatic contacts can survive continued military action.

stories.headline: NASA's Swift Observatory Plunges to Earth After 22-Year Mission
stories.summary:
NASA's Swift Observatory fell back to Earth on Wednesday, ending a 22-year investigation of the universe's biggest explosions. The U.S. Space Force confirmed the reentry near Indonesia after tracking the spacecraft's decaying orbit, which was driven by intense solar activity in recent years. It was not immediately known how much of the 1.5-ton spacecraft burned up, though NASA anticipated some denser pieces would survive.

Swift launched in 2004 for what was meant to be a two-year study of gamma ray bursts and exploding stars. It observed thousands of them and acted as a first responder for other telescopes that could probe deeper. Its end came less than three months after a long-shot rescue mission failed: NASA hired Katalyst Space for an orbit-boosting effort, but the company's robotic craft ran into trouble after its July launch and came down in September.

NASA is now gauging industry interest in a rescue of the Hubble Space Telescope, whose orbit is also being eroded by solar storms. Hubble, launched in 1990, is expected to fall by the mid-2030s, and any mission would need to happen by 2032. NASA is asking private companies whether they could boost its orbit, upgrade its systems or guide it to a controlled reentry.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said Hubble "still has important science ahead of it" and that the agency should look at every reasonable opportunity to keep it working. Science mission chief Nicky Fox said that, unlike the rushed Swift effort, there is more time to weigh options for Hubble.
